prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: a severe immunocompromised state (intravenous cyclophosphamide 10 days ago with prednisolone restarted at 60 mg daily) is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.

Do not attribute the deterioration to a flare of the presumed CNS vasculitis or escalate immunosuppression for it: fever, meningism and a neutrophilic CSF with a glucose ratio of 0.04 indicate bacterial meningitis.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 (61 years), diabetes mellitus and immunosuppressive therapy (prednisolone and cyclophosphamide) (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.

Hold prednisolone while dexamethasone is given and resume it at the end of the dexamethasone course without abrupt withdrawal; withhold further cyclophosphamide until the infection is controlled and the basis of the presumed CNS vasculitis has been reassessed.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (intravenous cyclophosphamide 10 days ago with prednisolone restarted at 60 mg daily) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: Streptococcus pneumoniae resistant to penicillin by meningitis breakpoints (MIC 0.12 mg/L) and susceptible to ceftriaxone (MIC 0.5 mg/L or less), so stop ampicillin and any vancomycin and continue ceftriaxone.
Stop metformin and glipizide and control glucose with insulin during dexamethasone (glucose 287 mg/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL).
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (intravenous cyclophosphamide 10 days ago with prednisolone restarted at 60 mg daily) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Corticosteroids blunt fever and meningism; in a patient on immunosuppression a low-grade fever with depressed consciousness warrants lumbar puncture rather than attribution to the underlying inflammatory disease.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gram-stain sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025); the multiplex PCR detects Streptococcus pneumoniae and both blood culture sets grow it.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lower the index of suspicion for bacterial meningitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatremia (129 mEq/L, about 132 after correction for a glucose of 287 mg/dL) is common in bacterial meningitis and in hyperglycemia and does not point away from meningitis; assess volume status before any fluid restriction, which is not routine in bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: a severe immunocompromised state (intravenous cyclophosphamide 10 days ago with high-dose prednisolone). NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (immunosuppressive therapy places him outside its scope). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025).

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate - patient with complex prior neurological history including presumed CNS vasculitis and recent immunosuppressive therapy now presenting with acute bacterial meningitis. The prior diagnosis of vasculitis creates diagnostic anchoring bias, steroid use confounds interpretation of inflammatory markers and WBC, and the negative CSF Gram stain leaves the organism to the PCR and blood cultures. Multiple comorbidities (diabetes, CKD) add management complexity.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kemal Yilmaz is a 61-year-old right-handed man with a complex neurological history who presents to the emergency department with acute worsening of speech, progressive somnolence, inability to walk, and new-onset fever over the past 48 hours. His wife reports that approximately eight months ago he was hospitalized for progressive headaches, slowed speech, gait unsteadiness, and generalized weakness. At that time, extensive workup was undertaken including brain imaging and lumbar puncture. His initial cerebrospinal fluid analysis reportedly showed a predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and low glucose. Workup for tuberculosis, lymphoma, paraneoplastic syndromes, and fungal infection were all reported as negative. Imaging at that time revealed small scattered gliotic lesions and some leptomeningeal enhancement, as well as acute ischemic lesions in the right caudate nucleus and left internal capsule, for which aspirin was initiated. Cerebral angiography showed hypoplastic vascular segments but no definitive vasculitis. Despite the inconclusive findings, a presumptive diagnosis of central nervous system vasculitis was made and he was treated with a 7-day intravenous methylprednisolone pulse followed by an oral prednisolone taper. He had shown modest improvement after that steroid course but never returned to his baseline neurological function, continuing to have mild dysarthria and requiring a cane to walk. Ten days before this presentation, because of these persisting deficits, prednisolone was restarted at 60 mg daily, since tapered to 20 mg daily, and he received a first dose of intravenous cyclophosphamide. Over the past two days, his wife noticed rapid deterioration: his speech became nearly unintelligible, he became increasingly drowsy and difficult to arouse, and he could no longer stand even with assistance. Yesterday evening she measured his temperature at 38.3 degrees Celsius. He had no clear response to acetaminophen. This morning he was minimally responsive, prompting her to call emergency services. She specifically denies any seizure-like activity, urinary incontinence, or recent falls. She notes that his diabetes control, already poor, has worsened since prednisolone was restarted, with home blood glucose readings frequently above 250 mg/dL. He has not had recent sick contacts or known exposures.
